summary: Defines a generalized change to distance vector routing protocols such as RIP, so they work well on demand circuits that are only connected when there is traffic.

eli5.summary: Instead of calling every minute, a router only talks when its news changes. That saves money on dial-up links.

questions: how does rip work on isdn
subtitle: Letting RIP-style routers on dial-up and X.25 links talk only when their routing news changes, with acknowledgements to make sure it arrives.

tldr.problem: Periodic routing broadcasts keep expensive X.25 or ISDN circuits open to every neighbour, and can fail to reach all of them when there are more neighbours than available channels.
tldr.mechanism: Routers send routing information only when their database changes or a circuit comes up, using three new packet types (triggered request, response and acknowledgement) with sequence numbers, fragmenting and retransmission.
tldr.outcome: Routing on demand circuits no longer needs a permanently open connection to each peer, while the protocols run unmodified on LANs and fixed point-to-point links. It is a Proposed Standard with no recorded replacement.

today: RFC 1582 is a Proposed Standard published in February 1994, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the RIP specifications of RFC 1058 and RFC 1388.

sections.title: Why Periodic Updates Hurt on a WAN
sections.content:
On connection oriented networks such as X.25 and ISDN, circuits are set up on demand and released when traffic subsides. Standard RIP sends its routing information to every next hop router every 30 seconds, so a circuit has to stay open to each destination. With N routers on the WAN, N * (N - 1) updates are sent over N * (N - 1)/2 connections every broadcast period.

The RFC lists three problems. It is expensive, because there are often minimum call charges. The number of routers can exceed the number of simultaneous calls the interface supports (a basic rate ISDN interface supports 2), so some neighbours never hear the update. And since the WAN has no broadcast, the update is queued separately for every neighbour, which can fill the transmit queue on a slow link.

The fix is to send routing information on the WAN only when the routing database changes or the circuit manager reports a change in reachability.
sections.eli5: If you had to call every friend every half minute to say 'nothing new', your phone bill would be huge and your phone line would be busy. It is better to call only when something changes.

sections.title: Triggered Updates and the Circuit Manager
sections.content:
A circuit manager sits between the connectionless network layers (IP, IPX and others) and the connection oriented WAN. It opens a virtual circuit to the next hop router when datagrams need to go there, and an idle timer closes it when they stop.

Routing responses are sent only in three cases: when a specific request arrives, when the routing database is modified by information from another interface, or when the circuit manager reports that a destination went from unreachable (circuit down) to reachable (circuit up). Changed information is not propagated at once but is delayed for a few seconds so several updates can be grouped.

Entries learned from a triggered response are presumed reachable until proven otherwise. The circuit manager sends an internal circuit down message if it fails to connect, and a circuit up message when it later succeeds, after which the two routers re-prime each other's databases. A router may keep a list of WAN peers, each marked as running the standard periodic protocol or the triggered one. Packets from a destination that does not support the expected variant MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: A helper watches the phone lines and tells the router when a neighbour can or cannot be reached. The router assumes what the neighbour said is still true until the helper says otherwise.

sections.title: Packet Types, Acknowledgement and Fragmentation
sections.content:
Three new packet types MUST be supported. A triggered request asks the peer for all appropriate parts of its routing database; it is sent at power on, when a destination returns after being down a long time, and when update fragments fail to arrive. A triggered response carries the database, leaving out entries learned from the interface it is sent on (split horizon), and it MUST be sent even if there is nothing to propagate. A triggered acknowledgement is sent for every response packet received.

Delivery is guaranteed by retransmitting a response until it is acknowledged. If the database changes first, a new update with a different sequence number goes out and an acknowledgement of the old one is ignored. A router updates its database only once it has a complete update, which may be several fragments, each individually acknowledged. If all fragments do not arrive within four times the retransmit period they are discarded and a triggered request is sent, which makes the originator resend all fragments. Any different sequence number means a newer update; the number carries no age.

After 10 retransmissions with no acknowledgement, routes via that peer are marked unreachable for a hold down period, and the peer is polled at a lower rate with triggered requests. At least 5 unacknowledged polls should be sent before the peer is marked as not supporting the mechanism. To avoid queue overload, a router MAY limit how many requests and responses are outstanding at once, but should always acknowledge immediately.
sections.eli5: Every message gets a 'got it' reply. If the reply does not come, the sender tries again. Long messages are cut into numbered pieces, and the receiver waits until it has all the pieces before using them.

sections.title: The Routing Database
sections.content:
Triggered updates only work if no routing information is ever lost, so the routing database MUST either keep all alternative routes it learns from the LAN and WAN, or keep some (say a best route and two alternatives). In the second case the router notes that it discarded something, and if the kept routes vanish it MUST issue a request on all interfaces to recover the alternatives. The RFC recommends doing this before all routes to a destination are lost.

Entries learned from LAN broadcasts are temporary and expire unless refreshed. Entries learned from a triggered response on the WAN are permanent and MUST NOT time out normally. They turn temporary when an update marks them unreachable, when an update omits them, or when the circuit manager reports it cannot connect. Poisoned reverse is also described: some routes learned from a peer are sent back to it marked unreachable, but only if they are the best route.
sections.eli5: The router keeps a notebook of every route it hears about, even backup ones, because nobody will repeat them later. It only crosses a route out when told it is gone or when the neighbour seems unreachable.

sections.title: Packet Formats for RIP, Netware RIP and SAP
sections.content:
The memo applies to IP RIP version 1, IP RIP version 2, Netware RIP and the Netware Service Advertising Protocol (SAP). IP RIP uses UDP port 520. In RIP the new commands are 6 (triggered request), 7 (triggered response) and 8 (triggered acknowledgement). Commands 7 and 8 add four octets after the header: a 2-octet sequence number, a 1-octet fragment number and a 1-octet number of fragments.

The sequence number MUST be incremented every time updated information is sent out on a WAN and wraps at 65535. An acknowledgement copies the sequence and fragment numbers of the response it acknowledges. The fragment number starts at one. A fragment holds up to 25 routing entries of 20 octets each in IP RIP, 50 entries of 8 octets in Netware RIP, and 8 service entries of 66 octets in SAP.

For RIP version 2, a triggered request carries the same four extra octets set to zero, and the security information MUST be appended to requests, acknowledgements and responses. Netware RIP uses IPX socket 453h and SAP uses socket 452h, with the same new operation values 6, 7 and 8.
sections.eli5: The messages get a few extra boxes on the front: a message number, 'this is piece 2', and 'there are 3 pieces'. Replies copy those numbers so the sender knows which piece was received.

sections.title: Timers
sections.content:
Three timers are used: the database timers, the retransmission timer and the reassembly timer. For IP RIP the suggested values are a 120 second hold down timer (matching RIP on broadcast networks), a 180 second database entry timer, a 5 second retransmission timer and a 20 second reassembly timer, four times the retransmission value.

When the circuit manager says a peer cannot be contacted, its routes start timing out as if learned by a normal response, are then advertised as unreachable during the hold down time, and are finally deleted. If the peer becomes reachable again while the entry timer runs, the routes are reinstated as permanent. If the entry timer already expired, the router MUST issue a triggered request.

Implementations MAY make the values configurable, but interoperability requires that all timers on a sub-network be the same in all routers. After 10 retransmissions the peer is polled every 60 seconds, for an administrator-defined number of polls of 5 or greater.
sections.eli5: Timers decide how long to wait before asking again, how long to keep a route after a neighbour goes quiet, and how long to wait for missing pieces. Everyone has to use the same clock settings.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Notes
sections.content:
The design assumes the circuit manager and the routing application are tightly bound. If they can run or crash independently, a keep-alive mechanism MUST exist between them so they can resynchronize. If the application believes the circuit manager has died, it marks all routes via it unreachable and advertises that for the hold down time before deleting them.

Security rests on address lists. The circuit manager needs a list of physical addresses to call and SHOULD accept incoming calls only from that list. The routing task MUST have a list of logical addresses to send triggered updates to, and the list doubles as the set of routers from which updates are accepted; anything from a router not on it MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: A router keeps a guest list. It only calls the people on the list and only listens to news from people on the list.

messages.label: TRIGGERED REQUEST (6)
messages.note: Asks for the routing database; repeated until a response arrives.

messages.label: TRIGGERED RESPONSE (7)
messages.note: Carries routes, possibly in several fragments.

messages.label: TRIGGERED ACKNOWLEDGEMENT (8)
messages.note: One per fragment, copying sequence and fragment numbers.

items.label: TRIGGERED REQUEST
items.desc: Asks the peer to send all of its routing database.

items.label: TRIGGERED RESPONSE
items.desc: Carries routing entries; has sequence, fragment and number-of-fragments fields.

items.label: TRIGGERED ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
items.desc: Sent for every response packet received.
